name: mean_variance_optimal_5s
author: adapted from claude-4.6-opus-agent-4
thesis: Markowitz mean-variance optimization can be applied to intraday entry timing by computing rolling expected return (EMA of 1-min returns) and rolling variance (realized variance over 30 bars) for a stock, then entering when the instantaneous Sharpe ratio (expected return / sqrt(variance)) exceeds a threshold. The intuition is that favorable risk/reward moments are transient — they appear when a stock has positive momentum but temporarily compressed volatility (coiled spring). The inefficiency exists because mean-variance optimization is used for portfolio allocation, not trade timing. Retail traders use static indicators; computing rolling risk-adjusted signals at 1-min frequency requires quantitative infrastructure.
mechanism: Institutional order flow arrives in bursts via algorithmic execution (TWAP/VWAP slicing), creating persistent directional pressure over 30-120 seconds. Retail and smaller participants follow the initial move, extending momentum before liquidity absorbs the flow and the order book rebalances.

conditions: Instant_Sharpe > 2.0 (rolling risk-adjusted return is strongly positive)
Sharpe_Percentile > 0.90 (current Sharpe is in top 10% of recent 2-hour window)
Instant_Sharpe < -2.0 (rolling risk-adjusted return is strongly negative)

exit.signal_exit: Instant_Sharpe crosses zero against position direction

weaknesses: Instant Sharpe on 1-min returns is extremely noisy — a single large bar can spike the Sharpe to > 2.0 and the confirmation bar check may not be sufficient to filter noise
Variance computed on 30 1-min returns is statistically unreliable; 30 data points give very wide confidence intervals on the variance estimate
The strategy assumes stationary return distributions within the 30-bar window, which is violated during news events, creating false high-Sharpe signals right before large adverse moves
prior_art: Markowitz (1952) mean-variance framework; applied to trade timing rather than portfolio construction; Lo (2002) on time-varying Sharpe ratios; rolling Sharpe used in portfolio analytics but not typically for entry signals
adaptation_notes: Converted from 1min to 5s bars. Lookback multiplier: 12x. Adaptations: timeframe scaling to 5-second candles; signal conversion from individual stock to NIFTY/BANKNIFTY index; lookback period scaling for 5-second bars. Stop/target calibrated for options point-based exits. Universe narrowed to NIFTY index.
